# Acts 23: verse-by-verse research notes

**Gaps you should know about:** Several pages couldn't be opened, so these notes are uneven. Verses 1–11 are well covered. Verses 12–35 are thinner. The Enduring Word page broke off after v. 11, and I only have short search extracts for the rest. I found nothing on vv. 7–9 beyond Enduring Word, and almost nothing on vv. 31–35. I found no material from Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan sites, Pentecostal sites other than enduringword.com, bibleodyssey.org or Catholic sites. I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Where I name a commentator's tradition (for example "Presbyterian"), that comes from StudyLight's own labels.

---

**v. 1 (good conscience)**
- Guzik says Paul wasn't claiming to be sinless. He meant that when his conscience showed him he was wrong, he responded and put things right. Guzik also quotes F.F. Bruce: a clear conscience was no basis for being justified before God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
- Barclay points out that "Brothers" put Paul on an equal footing with the court. The usual way to address the council was "Rulers of the people and elders of Israel." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/acts-23.html
- Chrysostom (Orthodox) reads it as Paul saying he knew of nothing he had done to wrong them or to deserve chains. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210148.htm

**v. 2 (Ananias orders the blow)**
- Guzik suggests two possible motives. Ananias may have been offended that an accused man claimed a clear conscience, or he may have felt convicted by Paul's integrity. Guzik notes that Josephus says Ananias stole tithes meant for the ordinary priests. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
- BibleHub's summary describes Ananias son of Nedebaeus (high priest AD 47–59) as notorious for greed and violence. https://biblehub.com/acts/23.htm
- Constable says Jewish law treated a man as innocent until proven guilty, yet Ananias punished Paul before any charge was made. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-3.html

**v. 3 ("whitewashed wall")**
- Shared reading: the phrase means hypocrisy. Barnes calls it a proverbial expression for "hypocrite." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-3.html
- Background: the image echoes Ezekiel 13:10–16 and Jesus' "whitewashed tombs" (Matthew 23:27). The NET Bible note, as quoted on Precept Austin, calls it an idiom for hypocrisy and also cites Deuteronomy 28:22. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-23-commentary
- Why the blow was illegal: Guzik cites Deuteronomy 25:1–2, which allows beating only a man found guilty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
- Fulfilment: Ellicott notes the words came true when the sicarii (Jewish assassins) killed Ananias some years later, citing Josephus. https://biblehub.com/acts/23-3.htm
- **Debate: was Paul's anger sinful?**
  - Matthew Henry: Paul spoke from holy zeal against abuse of power, with something of a prophetic spirit, and not from sinful passion or revenge. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-3.html
  - Ellicott: by Paul's own admission it was a hasty outburst that he took back after a moment's thought. https://biblehub.com/acts/23-3.htm
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel): Paul "lost his cool" and didn't turn the other cheek. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-3.html
  - Guzik leaves the tone open but says the rebuke was accurate and justified. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
  - Chrysostom: "this is not abuse." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210148.htm

**v. 4**
- Precept Austin quotes TDNT (Hanse): the high priest stands before God, and abusing him, especially while he is acting in office, counts as blasphemy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-23-commentary

**v. 5 ("I was not aware he was the high priest"): the main point of disagreement**
Interpreters have long disagreed here. Barnes says they "have been greatly divided." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-5.html
- **He didn't recognise Ananias.** Paul had been away for years and high priests changed often (Clarke). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-5.html Guzik also mentions the view that Paul had poor eyesight, inferred from Galatians 4 and 6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/ Chuck Smith leans toward the eyesight explanation, while Coffman (Restoration Movement) rejects it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/acts-23.html
- **Chrysostom (Orthodox):** he was fully convinced Paul really did not know. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210148.htm The ccel.org edition adds that a different text tradition of the homily speaks of a deliberate "economy" (holding back on purpose). https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf111.vi.xlviii.html
- **Calvin (Reformed):** rejects the idea that Paul simply didn't know, because the high priest held the chief seat in the council. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-5.html Schaff's note says Calvin's view is that Paul refused to recognise so unjust a man as a true high priest. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf111.vi.xlviii.html
- **Barnes (Presbyterian):** the office was vacant at the time, and Ananias was presiding by courtesy as a former high priest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-5.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Paul knew perfectly well who Ananias was but didn't stop to think in the moment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-5.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** gives practical reasons why Paul might not have known him. He also offers an alternative: since the priesthood had changed and Christ is now the only high priest of God, Paul did not acknowledge Ananias as one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/23-5.htm
- **Barclay:** reads it as irony, meaning "I never knew a man like that could be high priest." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-2.html
- **Application (BibleHub):** Paul's quick quotation of Exodus 22:28 shows him submitting to Scripture even under provocation. https://biblehub.com/acts/23.htm

**v. 6 ("I am a Pharisee")**
- Guzik: Paul saw the council wasn't open to the gospel and tried to protect his freedom by dividing it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
- **Debate: was the tactic honest and right?**
  - Ellicott asks frankly whether it was entirely truthful. His answer: there was no concealment, because Paul was standing with what was truest in Pharisee belief, and the resurrection of Jesus completes their hope. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/23-6.htm
  - Barnes calls it "a masterstroke of policy." He answers deist critics who called it dissimulation by noting that Paul never denied being a Christian and the resurrection really was central to his preaching. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/23-6.htm
  - Matthew Henry calls it "justifiable"; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown call it "quite warrantable." Poole calls it serpent-like wisdom used with dove-like innocence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/23-6.htm
  - Gill notes that Paul says "I *am* a Pharisee," not "I was," because he still held their beliefs that agree with Christianity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/23-6.htm
  - Guzik, by contrast, thinks Paul later suggested in Acts 24:20–21 that this had been "wrongdoing." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
  - Jack Arnold, quoted on Precept Austin, thinks Paul simply wanted to preach Jesus' resurrection. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-23-commentary

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik calls the Sadducees the liberals of their day. The Pharisees took Scripture seriously but added human traditions to it. Guzik also notes the two parties usually hated each other yet united against Jesus and Paul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
- Benson suggests the Sadducees may have read the angel passages in Moses allegorically, and denied that the soul lives on after death (citing Josephus). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/23-6.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: the Pharisees were going back to their teacher Gamaliel's advice in Acts 5:38–39. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/

**v. 10**
- Guzik: the day before, the crowd rioted over one word, "Gentiles"; now the council fought over one word, "resurrection." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
- Coffman: the commander was still completely in the dark about what lay behind the disturbances. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/acts-23.html

**v. 11 (the Lord stands by Paul)**
- Barnes: "the Lord" is clearly Jesus, and his appearing showed he approved of how Paul had acted before the council. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/23-11.htm
- Meyer: we can't tell whether this was a dream or a waking vision. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/23-11.htm Guzik thinks it seems to have been a physical presence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
- Guzik: in the New Testament the word for "take courage" is used only by Jesus, and the promise of Rome meant Paul had to survive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
- Spurgeon-style sermon material on BibleHub: the main comfort is that there is more work for Paul to do. https://biblehub.com/sermons/acts/23-11.htm
- Chuck Smith: the Lord came to comfort Paul, not to scold him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Act/Act_180.cfm

**vv. 12–15 (the oath)**
- Barclay calls the vow a *cherem*, meaning "May God curse me if I fail." He says the Jews regarded killing someone who endangered public morals as justifiable in some cases. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-13.html
- Guzik links the plotters to the dagger-carrying assassins of the time, and points out that they were willing to lie to reach a supposedly godly goal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
- Calvin: so many joining the plot shows how eager people are to do evil. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-12.html

**vv. 16–22 (Paul's nephew)**
- Guzik: this was no accident; God had to protect Paul because of the promise in v. 11. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
- Matthew Henry: Providence brought the plot to light. Chuck Smith says God works supernaturally through natural means. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-12.html

**vv. 23–24 (the escort)**
- Coffman: 470 men left at 9 p.m., ahead of any request from the priests and too large a force for the plotters to attack. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/acts-23.html
- Barclay: the scale of the escort shows the lengths Rome went to for a citizen. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/23-13.html

**vv. 25–30 (Lysias's letter)**
- Coffman sees it as a self-serving distortion: Lysias only found out Paul was a Roman after binding him illegally. He also suggests the name "Claudius" may have been taken to honour the emperor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/acts-23.html
- Guzik agrees the letter leaves out the near-scourging. He thinks Luke's key line is "nothing deserving death or chains," possibly written for Paul's trial before Caesar. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/
- Barclay, unusually, calls the letter completely fair and impartial. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/acts-23.html

**vv. 31–33**
- Guzik: Paul got out of Jerusalem and the plot failed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-23/

**vv. 34–35**
- Barclay: Caesarea was the seat of Roman government, and Herod the Great built the palace there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/acts-23.html
